A newly established test facility at Sandia National Laboratories successfully tested a modular silicon carbide (SiC) ceramic air receiver designed by GE Aerospace Research, achieving near world-record temperatures of approximately 1,400°C. The breakthrough opens avenues for low- cost, high-temperature thermal energy systems applicable in industrial processes such as ammonia production and mineral processing. The advanced receiver, known as HOTSSTAR, was developed in collaboration with Heliogen and leverages GE Aerospace's expertise in additive manufacturing and ceramic matrix composites. This technology could enhance energy resilience in the U.S. by providing a reliable alternative energy source for high-temperature industrial processes, thereby supporting sectors like cement and steel manufacturing. The successful tests at Sandia's National Solar Thermal Test Facility highlight the potential for improved efficiency and reduced costs in energy-intensive applications. SOLAR FURNACE HIGHLIGHTS Core Objective The NSTTF solar furnace is a renewable resource that provides a wide range of high heat test scenarios, thermal model validation tools, and environments for testing. The furnace can be outfitted with custom fixtures to emulate desired environments to fulfill our customers need. The facility has an adjustable platform to move your sample into place and, using a 120 m2 heliostat and a static parabolic dish, we can subject samples to up to 16 kW of thermal energy. This allows us to safely reach flux levels of 600 W/cm2 and temperatures of nearly 3000⁰ Celsius. As a unique facility, the NSTTF solar furnace is one of the few places in the U.S. that can provide solar calibration for flux gages and environments for thermal validation. It is configured to handle up to 32 thermocouples, 12 analog input and output channels for voltage and current measuring. Additionally, it has high-speed/high-resolution video cameras with light filtering, and gas and particulate capture techniques to aid in material analysis.
